accepted.excerpt: I am self-hosting my (secondary) email and have only implemented SPF and DKIM. This works fine on a practical level for me. What would be the benefit of setting up DMARC on top?

To this day none of the mail servers I’ve setup can send to verizon.net. It’s not “hard”, but there are servers who will not accept a single message from you, rDNS, DKIM/SPF be damned. And there’s fuck-all you can do about it.

market.summary: The relevant niche is DMARC software for organizations that need authentication visibility, policy guidance and remediation without specialist email staff. Published market estimates support meaningful demand, although their wide spread makes precise sizing uncertain. One estimate projects the market at [[ev:s_539586ac6fc8]], while another reports a measured market value of [[ev:s_a6ad63b48bd6]]. The latter source also projects substantial expansion [[ev:s_9be096491962]]. These claims indicate an established category with room for continued adoption, but they do not isolate web agencies, IT freelancers or small businesses. That narrower segment should therefore be treated as a promising wedge rather than a proven market share claim. The opportunity comes from translating machine-oriented aggregate reports, DNS records and policy behavior into client-facing explanations and safe changes. Agencies also create a natural account structure because one operator may oversee several unrelated domains, sending platforms and DNS providers. The product can sit between basic record checkers and broader deliverability suites by emphasizing plain-English diagnosis, guided remediation and portfolio monitoring. A focused service does not need to replace every deliverability tool. It needs to make recurring DMARC work understandable, actionable and easy to communicate to a client who lacks an email administrator.

community.summary: The community evidence shows confusion at several layers of email operations. A self-hoster who already configured SPF and DKIM still asks what DMARC adds [[ev:q_b22b9ef2da41]], revealing that setup guidance often fails to explain purpose, policy and practical benefit. Another practitioner reports dealing with ticketing and marketing systems that misunderstand the roles of SPF, DKIM and DMARC [[ev:q_e9c3d589d88d]], which suggests that authentication failures can originate across a fragmented sending stack rather than one mail server. Deliverability pain is also experienced as an opaque outcome: one company believed Microsoft 365 mail had encountered a keyword blacklist [[ev:q_d93f6facccac]]. These are useful buyer signals because the problem is not merely reading an aggregate report. Operators need help connecting symptoms to senders, authentication alignment, DNS configuration and provider behavior. They also need language suitable for clients who want an answer and a remedy, not protocol theory.

goToMarket.positioning: MailPlain is the DMARC monitoring desk for web agencies, IT freelancers and owner-led businesses that need an answer they can act on. It converts authentication evidence into prioritized DNS guidance, identifies the likely sending service involved and produces client-ready explanations without requiring deep deliverability expertise.

goToMarket.pricingNotes: Price the product by monitored domain while making the agency package cheaper and easier than assembling many isolated subscriptions. Monitordmarc establishes paid entry and business anchors [[ev:p_eda00442ad6e]] [[ev:p_d78c1f1225f7]], while Uriports demonstrates an unusually low annual option for hobby use [[ev:p_9b0ac1fbc067]]. Mxtoolbox pairs free entry with materially broader paid offers [[ev:p_9aae92c90f68]] [[ev:p_a72083ebba67]]. MailPlain should charge for interpretation, guided remediation, client communication and portfolio workflow rather than raw report ingestion alone.

whyNow: DMARC software already has an established measured market and a growth outlook [[ev:s_a6ad63b48bd6]] [[ev:s_9be096491962]], yet practical understanding remains uneven. Operators still report that connected business systems misunderstand SPF, DKIM and DMARC [[ev:q_e9c3d589d88d]]. That combination supports a timely usability wedge: simplify an existing technical category for buyers who manage domains as one responsibility among many.
howItWorks: Connect Domain — The user adds a domain, confirms the reporting destination and follows provider-specific instructions for routing aggregate reports. MailPlain inspects the current SPF, DKIM and DMARC posture, maps visible senders and highlights configuration gaps without requiring the user to interpret raw XML.

Understand Senders — MailPlain groups authentication traffic by recognizable service, domain alignment and outcome. Instead of exposing protocol-heavy tables as the main interface, it explains which system appears legitimate, which source needs investigation and why a failure may affect trust or delivery.

Apply the Fix — For each issue, MailPlain proposes a plain-English remediation path with the exact DNS record change, expected effect and rollback guidance. The user can copy a provider-ready value, request approval from a client and record when the change was published.

Prove the Result — After a change, MailPlain watches subsequent reports for alignment improvement, unexpected senders and policy impact. It creates a concise client summary showing what changed, what remains unresolved and which action deserves attention next, while retaining an audit trail for the agency.

editorial.dontBuildYet: Do not build a full outbound email platform, blacklist removal service or autonomous DNS writer before the monitoring and guided-remediation workflow earns trust.
editorial.problemNarrative:
Web agencies, IT freelancers and small-business owners routinely inherit responsibility for email authentication because they control DNS, maintain the website or administer Microsoft 365. They may not operate the mail infrastructure, understand every sending service or have a dedicated email administrator. When messages begin landing in spam, a client expects the technical contact to explain why. The available evidence often arrives as XML reports, unfamiliar source addresses, alignment results and policy terminology rather than a direct diagnosis.

Even the purpose of DMARC can remain unclear after SPF and DKIM are working. A self-hoster asks what benefit DMARC adds on top of those controls [[ev:q_b22b9ef2da41]]. That uncertainty matters because an operator may publish a record without understanding reporting, alignment or how policy changes affect legitimate senders. Fragmented software makes the task harder. One practitioner describes ticketing and marketing platforms that misunderstand SPF, DKIM and DMARC [[ev:q_e9c3d589d88d]]. A domain may therefore involve a mailbox provider, website forms, a help desk, invoicing software and a campaign platform, with no shared owner of authentication.

The visible symptom is often vague and urgent. A company encountering Microsoft 365 delivery trouble suspected a keyword blacklist [[ev:q_d93f6facccac]]. Without a clear workflow, the responsible freelancer may check DNS records, search blocklists, inspect headers and contact vendors without knowing which signal matters. Passing raw DMARC dashboards to the client does not resolve the communication problem. The buyer needs a prioritized explanation: which sender is failing, whether it appears legitimate, what DNS or platform setting should change and how to confirm that the repair worked.

Agencies face an added portfolio burden. Every client can use a different registrar, DNS host and sending stack. The operator needs separation between domains, a record of approvals and a concise status update that can be forwarded without rewriting protocol output. The core pain is therefore not simple report collection. It is converting scattered authentication evidence into a safe action and a credible client explanation before deliverability trouble damages confidence.
editorial.solutionNarrative:
MailPlain would be a per-domain DMARC monitoring service designed around diagnosis and communication rather than protocol dashboards. Its wedge is a plain-English issue feed that identifies the likely sending service, explains the authentication failure, proposes the exact DNS or platform change and shows how the operator can verify the result. The interface would prioritize actionable exceptions while keeping raw evidence available for technical review.

A user would connect a domain by publishing or updating a reporting address. MailPlain would ingest aggregate reports, normalize sender sources and correlate them with SPF, DKIM, alignment and current DNS records. Recognizable services would appear under human-readable labels. Unknown sources would enter a review queue where the user can mark them as approved, suspicious or needing client confirmation. Each diagnosis would include context about likely impact and a remediation checklist suited to the relevant DNS or sending provider.

For agencies, the product would add portfolio triage and client communication. A shared dashboard would show domains needing action, domains awaiting approval and domains that appear stable. A client-ready summary would explain the problem, recommended fix and observed result without exposing unnecessary XML detail. Approval links would let the client confirm a sender or authorize a proposed DNS change while leaving publication under the operator's control.

MailPlain should initially remain advisory. It can generate copyable record values, preserve previous configurations and monitor the effect of a change, but it should not silently edit production DNS. That boundary supports trust while the product learns how varied sender stacks behave. Over time, provider integrations can streamline implementation after the diagnosis, approval and verification loop is reliable.
editorial.competitiveNarrative: Monitordmarc already packages monitoring for small and growing businesses through distinct paid plans [[ev:p_eda00442ad6e]] [[ev:p_0ccf94f7234e]]. MailPlain would differentiate through agency workflow, client approvals and explanations centered on the exact remediation rather than presenting monitoring as the endpoint. Uriports offers a low-cost Sand plan [[ev:p_9b0ac1fbc067]], making it attractive for technically capable users who can interpret reports independently. MailPlain should not compete for hobbyist ingestion on price; it should serve operators who bill for resolving client problems. Mxtoolbox offers free access [[ev:p_9aae92c90f68]] alongside paid Delivery Center packages [[ev:p_a72083ebba67]] [[ev:p_ae198f0c2cf0]], reflecting a broader deliverability toolset. MailPlain can remain narrower: DMARC-centered diagnosis, DNS change guidance, sender approval and client-ready proof of resolution. The durable distinction is not another checker. It is a structured handoff from technical evidence to an approved fix across an agency portfolio.
editorial.stackNotes: Use a TypeScript application with Next.js for the dashboard and API routes, PostgreSQL for normalized authentication data, and a durable object store for original aggregate report files. A background queue should parse XML, enrich source addresses, refresh DNS records and generate summaries without blocking the interface. Isolate report ingestion from customer-facing requests, validate archive contents defensively and preserve parser errors for review. Add encrypted credentials for provider integrations, role-aware client approvals, immutable DNS change snapshots and structured observability around delayed reports, duplicate payloads and sender classification decisions.
editorial.brandBrief: Use a calm, diagnostic visual language that feels closer to a trusted IT worksheet than a security command center. Favor warm neutrals, crisp status colors, readable DNS snippets and generous spacing. Avoid fear-based shields, hacker imagery and dense protocol charts. The voice should be direct, reassuring and specific: explain the likely cause, name the safe next action and acknowledge uncertainty when evidence is incomplete. Client exports should look polished without feeling like automated marketing collateral.
